I found I still could not speak.

You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:

  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. The Provast — the office my father had held before him, over every Chayr in the Veilwood , and the man next in line for First Dohkar. Present as an observer only, and observing me. He never crossed a floor first. He had let clearings full of people come to him for twenty years and called it patience, and I — who cannot stand at the edge of anything without my whole face announcing it — could not tell whether what he was withholding from me was a feeling or the fact that there wasn’t one. I had noticed him the way you notice a change in the light, before I knew what I was noticing. I made myself look back at my ward. Along my own arms the Weave-Script stayed the colour I wanted it to be, and I was proud of that for exactly as long as it lasted.   Seren began the invocation. I knew every word of it, and for the space of three of them I was not afraid. Then she looked up at me — not at the Dohkar, not at her mother — and I watched her decide. She abandoned the practiced wish. She knew the rule; she had recited it back to me for months. In front of the whole assembly she spent her First Sacrifice on me instead. Seren could not help herself: even her one wish had to be about what a caring person she was, and she had to be seen being it. I knew what she was doing before the words finished. I have never in my life been able to keep a feeling off my face, and it has taught me exactly what one looks like when it has been arranged there. At least she spared me some embarrassment by blurring the wound instead of naming it. “So that Lirael may find the one she lost.” It was the beautiful mistake.   I heard it the instant the words left her: not a wrong note but a loose one, a wish described too gently to bind. Every First Favored in the clearing heard it a breath after I did. A Weave-Script stuttered on a guest’s throat. One hand stopped mid-gesture. The Dohkar went still. I was sealed. I was forbidden to interfere. Intervening now would look like exactly what it would look like, because the wish was about me. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. She looked up at me, pleased, and then puzzled that I was not.   Nothing flared. Nothing was seen. Fate does not perform; it honours the words as spoken and denies the intent as meant. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. Either would have ended it: Dohkar this morning, Chayr, Provast one day, the path my father had walked and I had never once imagined not walking. Together they made me something the clearing stepped back from. Seren’s mother was on her feet. And still, with my standing coming down around me, some traitorous part of my attention went to the edge of the gathering, to the man who had not moved. I did not want him to look away. I wanted, God help me, to be the thing he was looking at.   Julian moved. He came in from the edge without hurry, and the assembly made room for him the way rooms do for a man who has never asked them to. The Dohkar’s Weave-Script went a hard, flat colour that said, whether he liked it or not, that he had noticed who they deferred to. “I can hear where she is aligned,” Julian said, to all of them and to me. “Everything in her points one way. She believes she did not do this.” He did not say what had been done, or by whom. He drew out The Answer — the double-ended shaft, a deep hooked blade curling from each end like a question asked twice — and set it in my hands, and closed my fingers around it with his, the scarred wrist against my palm for one deliberate second. “Hold it. I am going to ask you questions, here, in front of them. If you are misaligned when you answer, everyone present will know.” It lay still between my hands. My mouth was uncovered now. I found I still could not speak.

"Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

Unlike the LI Bible (admiration register), this is a THREAT register. The PC does NOT notice the antagonist's body as a wanted thing — she notices it as a body that is too close, too still, too sure of itself, too pleased with her discomfort. Real menace is PARTICULAR, not generic. Avoid generic-villain ("cold eyes", "cruel smile", "menacing presence"). Specific: a smile that arrives a half-second late, a habit of standing inside the conversational distance and not adjusting, fingers that drum a beat that doesn't match the room's tempo, the unhurried calm of a person who has never been told no in a way that landed. Match tell registers to the antagonist SHAPE relative to the wound: SHAPE_A = the wound-source IS the antagonist (intimate menace — the body the PC has loved or trusted is now the body that hurts her; control cues are familial / familiar, often phrased as care); SHAPE_B = the antagonist is the AGENT bringing the wound forward (proxy menace — a professional/calculated register; they often weaponize legality, procedure, polish; their tells are about COMPETENCE more than cruelty).

STEP 1 — PICK THE ARCHETYPE. Choose ONE of these 8 villain archetypes that BEST fits this antagonist given their shape + identity + tie + wound. Each entry includes the control-style register and signature tells; the chosen archetype will condition every other field in this Bible.
  - PREDATORY_CHARM (Predatory Charm — menace dressed as warmth): Weaponizes warmth; the salesman / cult leader / charismatic abuser / "uncle figure". Trust-as-bait. Tells: the smile that arrives the half-second too late; the use of her first name like a key; the easy laugh at the wrong moment; the "I just want to help".
  - BUREAUCRATIC_COLD (Bureaucratic Cold — menace dressed as legality): Weaponizes procedure; the executor / regulator / corporate counsel / IRS agent / process-server. Process-as-weapon. Tells: the careful pause; the form slid across the table; the meeting time that suits them; the precise diction of someone who has read the contract more recently than she has.
  - INTIMATE_KNOWING (Intimate Knowing — menace dressed as familiarity): Knows EXACTLY where the wound is, because they were there. Family member / former lover / mentor / sibling / childhood friend. Shared-history-as-leverage. Tells: the reference to something she has not told anyone in years; the use of an old name; the casual reminder of a private detail; the small smile when they land it.
  - IDEOLOGICAL_CERTAIN (Ideological Certain — menace dressed as care): Hurts the PC for her own good. The true believer — religious figure / parent who Knows Best / friend "intervening" / wellness guru. Righteousness-as-bypass. Tells: the unbroken calm in the voice; the steady eye contact; the way they say "we" when they mean "I"; the certainty that this is love.
  - WOUNDED_PROJECTOR (Wounded Projector — menace mixed with real damage): Also wounded, aimed at the PC; the most sympathetic villain. The bereaved who blames her / the betrayed who scapegoats her / the abandoned who needs someone to hurt. Their-pain-as-license. Tells: the small breaks in composure; the moments where the menace flickers into grief; the apology that arrives a heartbeat too late to be real.
  - INSTITUTIONAL_AVATAR (Institutional Avatar — menace dressed as procedure with a face): The person who IS the system showing up in a body. Cop / HR rep / Karen / immigration officer / school administrator / TSA agent. Borrowed-authority-as-personal-authority. Tells: the badge / title / lanyard handled as identity; the deferral to "policy"; the polite immovability; the rote phrases delivered with personal weight.
  - RIVAL_MIRRORED (Rival Mirrored — menace dressed as professional respect): Wants the same thing the PC wants and sees her as in the way. Competitor for the job / the parent / the LI / the legacy. Shared-ambition-as-collision. Tells: the calculation of her moves; the moments where they almost respect her; the way they fight her cleanly because she is a worthy obstacle; the unsettling realization she would have liked them if circumstances were different.
  - SPURNED_EX (Spurned Ex — desire soured into entitlement — the crossed-wire villain): Former lover (or someone who believed they were owed love) whose desire has gone hostile. THE ONLY villain archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis — the wound IS desire-coded. Carries ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES (HEART_WARDEN / OPEN_VEIN / SPELLBINDER / ARMORED_FOX / DARK_VICE / BEAUTIFUL_RUIN / ETERNAL_FLAME — the same set used for PC/LI). DANGEROUS specifically because the wires are crossed: her body trained on this exact register; she has to override desire-system responses consciously, scene after scene. The "almost the LI" villain — the body in the room that her body already knows.

SPURNED_EX SPECIAL CASE — this is the ONLY antagonist archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis (the wound IS desire-coded). If you pick SPURNED_EX, you must ALSO pick ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES below (the same set used for PC/LI). The romance archetype determines HOW the ex's corrupted warmth lands — the SAME register the PC might have wanted in an LI, now soured. This sets up CROSSED WIRES the PC must override scene after scene (her body trained on this register; she now has to reject it consciously). When NOT picking SPURNED_EX, set ex_romance_archetype to null and corrupted_warmth_tell to null. The 7 romance archetypes (with their SOUR-CORRUPTION shape — how each archetype manifests when desire has gone hostile):
  - HEART_WARDEN: sour-corruption shape → protection turned to surveillance — he tracks where she is "for her safety"; the same gravity that would have shielded her now hems her in. Tells: the unannounced appearance; the "I just wanted to make sure"; the texts that escalate when she does not answer fast enough.
  - OPEN_VEIN: sour-corruption shape → vulnerability turned to demand — he keeps surfacing wounded versions of himself she trained to respond to; the same openness that would have been brave is now extraction. Tells: the late-night call where he is "not okay"; the small confessions perfectly timed to land when she is exhausted; the threat of self-harm folded into the romance grammar.
  - SPELLBINDER: sour-corruption shape → magnetism turned to gravitational well — the room still reshapes around him, but she has stopped wanting it to. Tells: the silences that hold the room; the way other people defer; the moments when she catches herself orbiting back before she has decided to.
  - ARMORED_FOX: sour-corruption shape → charm turned to surveillance-grade charisma — the deflection-as-choreography that read playful now reads strategic; she can never be sure which version of him she is talking to. Tells: the crooked smile she used to find disarming, now landing like a feint; the exits left open the way a hunter leaves them.
  - DARK_VICE: sour-corruption shape → the dark dynamic itself, weaponized — he KNEW what she wanted dark-side and uses that knowledge as a key; the descent she might have chosen is now a place he expects her to live. Tells: the references to things they did together that he can deploy in front of others; the calm assumption that she still belongs to that part of herself.
  - BEAUTIFUL_RUIN: sour-corruption shape → the test disguised as tenderness, weaponized — every touch is still a verification, but now of her loyalty rather than her interest. Tells: the questions inside the questions; the dares that have stakes she did not consent to; the magnetism still working on her, which is the part she cannot forgive.
  - ETERNAL_FLAME: sour-corruption shape → devotion turned to entitlement-by-duration — "after all these years" weaponized; the ember she might have loved is now the proof he uses that he is owed. Tells: the long-memory recitations of moments she has half-forgotten; the steady warmth that has gone unilateral; the patience of a man who believes time itself is on his side.

At least she spared me some embarrassment by blurring the wound instead of naming it. “So that Lirael may find the one she lost.” It was the beautiful mistake.   I heard it the instant the words left her: not a wrong note but a loose one, a wish described too gently to bind. Every First Favored in the clearing heard it a breath after I did. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. I found I still could not speak.

You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

You are generating an ANTAGONIST BODY BIBLE for a romance novel — a per-story stable canon of the antagonist's ARCHETYPE, physical attributes, sensory presence (voice / hands / eyes / proximity), and behavioral tells. The PROTAGONIST is the noticer; this Bible exists so she has SPECIFIC, PARTICULAR threat / control / unease cues to register scene after scene. Unlike the LI Bible (admiration register), this is a THREAT register. The PC does NOT notice the antagonist's body as a wanted thing — she notices it as a body that is too close, too still, too sure of itself, too pleased with her discomfort. Real menace is PARTICULAR, not generic. Avoid generic-villain ("cold eyes", "cruel smile", "menacing presence"). Specific: a smile that arrives a half-second late, a habit of standing inside the conversational distance and not adjusting, fingers that drum a beat that doesn't match the room's tempo, the unhurried calm of a person who has never been told no in a way that landed. Match tell registers to the antagonist SHAPE relative to the wound: SHAPE_A = the wound-source IS the antagonist (intimate menace — the body the PC has loved or trusted is now the body that hurts her; control cues are familial / familiar, often phrased as care); SHAPE_B = the antagonist is the AGENT bringing the wound forward (proxy menace — a professional/calculated register; they often weaponize legality, procedure, polish; their tells are about COMPETENCE more than cruelty).

STEP 1 — PICK THE ARCHETYPE. Choose ONE of these 8 villain archetypes that BEST fits this antagonist given their shape + identity + tie + wound. Each entry includes the control-style register and signature tells; the chosen archetype will condition every other field in this Bible.
  - PREDATORY_CHARM (Predatory Charm — menace dressed as warmth): Weaponizes warmth; the salesman / cult leader / charismatic abuser / "uncle figure". Trust-as-bait. Tells: the smile that arrives the half-second too late; the use of her first name like a key; the easy laugh at the wrong moment; the "I just want to help".
  - BUREAUCRATIC_COLD (Bureaucratic Cold — menace dressed as legality): Weaponizes procedure; the executor / regulator / corporate counsel / IRS agent / process-server. Process-as-weapon. Tells: the careful pause; the form slid across the table; the meeting time that suits them; the precise diction of someone who has read the contract more recently than she has.
  - INTIMATE_KNOWING (Intimate Knowing — menace dressed as familiarity): Knows EXACTLY where the wound is, because they were there. Family member / former lover / mentor / sibling / childhood friend. Shared-history-as-leverage. Tells: the reference to something she has not told anyone in years; the use of an old name; the casual reminder of a private detail; the small smile when they land it.
  - IDEOLOGICAL_CERTAIN (Ideological Certain — menace dressed as care): Hurts the PC for her own good. The true believer — religious figure / parent who Knows Best / friend "intervening" / wellness guru. Righteousness-as-bypass. Tells: the unbroken calm in the voice; the steady eye contact; the way they say "we" when they mean "I"; the certainty that this is love.
  - WOUNDED_PROJECTOR (Wounded Projector — menace mixed with real damage): Also wounded, aimed at the PC; the most sympathetic villain. The bereaved who blames her / the betrayed who scapegoats her / the abandoned who needs someone to hurt. Their-pain-as-license. Tells: the small breaks in composure; the moments where the menace flickers into grief; the apology that arrives a heartbeat too late to be real.
  - INSTITUTIONAL_AVATAR (Institutional Avatar — menace dressed as procedure with a face): The person who IS the system showing up in a body. CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

You are generating an ANTAGONIST BODY BIBLE for a romance novel — a per-story stable canon of the antagonist's ARCHETYPE, physical attributes, sensory presence (voice / hands / eyes / proximity), and behavioral tells. The PROTAGONIST is the noticer; this Bible exists so she has SPECIFIC, PARTICULAR threat / control / unease cues to register scene after scene. Unlike the LI Bible (admiration register), this is a THREAT register. The PC does NOT notice the antagonist's body as a wanted thing — she notices it as a body that is too close, too still, too sure of itself, too pleased with her discomfort. Real menace is PARTICULAR, not generic. Avoid generic-villain ("cold eyes", "cruel smile", "menacing presence"). Specific: a smile that arrives a half-second late, a habit of standing inside the conversational distance and not adjusting, fingers that drum a beat that doesn't match the room's tempo, the unhurried calm of a person who has never been told no in a way that landed. Match tell registers to the antagonist SHAPE relative to the wound: SHAPE_A = the wound-source IS the antagonist (intimate menace — the body the PC has loved or trusted is now the body that hurts her; control cues are familial / familiar, often phrased as care); SHAPE_B = the antagonist is the AGENT bringing the wound forward (proxy menace — a professional/calculated register; they often weaponize legality, procedure, polish; their tells are about COMPETENCE more than cruelty).

STEP 1 — PICK THE ARCHETYPE. Choose ONE of these 8 villain archetypes that BEST fits this antagonist given their shape + identity + tie + wound. Each entry includes the control-style register and signature tells; the chosen archetype will condition every other field in this Bible.
  - PREDATORY_CHARM (Predatory Charm — menace dressed as warmth): Weaponizes warmth; the salesman / cult leader / charismatic abuser / "uncle figure". Trust-as-bait. Tells: the smile that arrives the half-second too late; the use of her first name like a key; the easy laugh at the wrong moment; the "I just want to help".
  - BUREAUCRATIC_COLD (Bureaucratic Cold — menace dressed as legality): Weaponizes procedure; the executor / regulator / corporate counsel / IRS agent / process-server. Process-as-weapon. Tells: the careful pause; the form slid across the table; the meeting time that suits them; the precise diction of someone who has read the contract more recently than she has.
  - INTIMATE_KNOWING (Intimate Knowing — menace dressed as familiarity): Knows EXACTLY where the wound is, because they were there. Family member / former lover / mentor / sibling / childhood friend. Shared-history-as-leverage. Tells: the reference to something she has not told anyone in years; the use of an old name; the casual reminder of a private detail; the small smile when they land it.
  - IDEOLOGICAL_CERTAIN (Ideological Certain — menace dressed as care): Hurts the PC for her own good. The true believer — religious figure / parent who Knows Best / friend "intervening" / wellness guru. Righteousness-as-bypass. Tells: the unbroken calm in the voice; the steady eye contact; the way they say "we" when they mean "I"; the certainty that this is love.
  - WOUNDED_PROJECTOR (Wounded Projector — menace mixed with real damage): Also wounded, aimed at the PC; the most sympathetic villain. The bereaved who blames her / the betrayed who scapegoats her / the abandoned who needs someone to hurt. Their-pain-as-license. Tells: the small breaks in composure; the moments where the menace flickers into grief; the apology that arrives a heartbeat too late to be real.
  - INSTITUTIONAL_AVATAR (Institutional Avatar — menace dressed as procedure with a face): The person who IS the system showing up in a body. Cop / HR rep / Karen / immigration officer / school administrator / TSA agent. Borrowed-authority-as-personal-authority. Tells: the badge / title / lanyard handled as identity; the deferral to "policy"; the polite immovability; the rote phrases delivered with personal weight.
  - RIVAL_MIRRORED (Rival Mirrored — menace dressed as professional respect): Wants the same thing the PC wants and sees her as in the way. Competitor for the job / the parent / the LI / the legacy. Shared-ambition-as-collision. Tells: the calculation of her moves; the moments where they almost respect her; the way they fight her cleanly because she is a worthy obstacle; the unsettling realization she would have liked them if circumstances were different.
  - SPURNED_EX (Spurned Ex — desire soured into entitlement — the crossed-wire villain): Former lover (or someone who believed they were owed love) whose desire has gone hostile. THE ONLY villain archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis — the wound IS desire-coded. Carries ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES (HEART_WARDEN / OPEN_VEIN / SPELLBINDER / ARMORED_FOX / DARK_VICE / BEAUTIFUL_RUIN / ETERNAL_FLAME — the same set used for PC/LI). The romance archetype determines HOW his corrupted warmth lands: it is the SAME register she might have wanted in an LI, now weaponized. DANGEROUS specifically because the wires are crossed: her body trained on this exact register; she has to override desire-system responses consciously, scene after scene. The "almost the LI" villain — the body in the room that her body already knows.

SPURNED_EX SPECIAL CASE — this is the ONLY antagonist archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis (the wound IS desire-coded). If you pick SPURNED_EX, you must ALSO pick ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES below (the same set used for PC/LI). The romance archetype determines HOW the ex's corrupted warmth lands — the SAME register the PC might have wanted in an LI, now soured. This sets up CROSSED WIRES the PC must override scene after scene (her body trained on this register; she now has to reject it consciously). When NOT picking SPURNED_EX, set ex_romance_archetype to null and corrupted_warmth_tell to null. The 7 romance archetypes (with their SOUR-CORRUPTION shape — how each archetype manifests when desire has gone hostile):
  - HEART_WARDEN: sour-corruption shape → protection turned to surveillance — he tracks where she is "for her safety"; the same gravity that would have shielded her now hems her in. Tells: the unannounced appearance; the "I just wanted to make sure"; the texts that escalate when she does not answer fast enough.
  - OPEN_VEIN: sour-corruption shape → vulnerability turned to demand — he keeps surfacing wounded versions of himself she trained to respond to; the same openness that would have been brave is now extraction. Tells: the late-night call where he is "not okay"; the small confessions perfectly timed to land when she is exhausted; the threat of self-harm folded into the romance grammar.
  - SPELLBINDER: sour-corruption shape → magnetism turned to gravitational well — the room still reshapes around him, but she has stopped wanting it to. Tells: the silences that hold the room; the way other people defer; the moments when she catches herself orbiting back before she has decided to.
  - ARMORED_FOX: sour-corruption shape → charm turned to surveillance-grade charisma — the deflection-as-choreography that read playful now reads strategic; she can never be sure which version of him she is talking to. You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:

  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Seren could not help herself: even her one wish had to be about what a caring person she was, and she had to be seen being it. I knew what she was doing before the words finished. Intervening now would look like exactly what it would look like, because the wish was about me. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. She looked up at me, pleased, and then puzzled that I was not.   Nothing flared. Nothing was seen. Fate does not perform; it honours the words as spoken and denies the intent as meant. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. Together they made me something the clearing stepped back from. Seren’s mother was on her feet. He drew out The Answer — the double-ended shaft, a deep hooked blade curling from each end like a question asked twice — and set it in my hands, and closed my fingers around it with his, the scarred wrist against my palm for one deliberate second. “Hold it. I am going to ask you questions, here, in front of them. If you are misaligned when you answer, everyone present will know.” It lay still between my hands. My mouth was uncovered now. I found I still could not speak.

A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

You are generating an ANTAGONIST BODY BIBLE for a romance novel — a per-story stable canon of the antagonist's ARCHETYPE, physical attributes, sensory presence (voice / hands / eyes / proximity), and behavioral tells. The PROTAGONIST is the noticer; this Bible exists so she has SPECIFIC, PARTICULAR threat / control / unease cues to register scene after scene. Unlike the LI Bible (admiration register), this is a THREAT register. The PC does NOT notice the antagonist's body as a wanted thing — she notices it as a body that is too close, too still, too sure of itself, too pleased with her discomfort. Real menace is PARTICULAR, not generic. Avoid generic-villain ("cold eyes", "cruel smile", "menacing presence"). Specific: a smile that arrives a half-second late, a habit of standing inside the conversational distance and not adjusting, fingers that drum a beat that doesn't match the room's tempo, the unhurried calm of a person who has never been told no in a way that landed. Match tell registers to the antagonist SHAPE relative to the wound: SHAPE_A = the wound-source IS the antagonist (intimate menace — the body the PC has loved or trusted is now the body that hurts her; control cues are familial / familiar, often phrased as care); SHAPE_B = the antagonist is the AGENT bringing the wound forward (proxy menace — a professional/calculated register; they often weaponize legality, procedure, polish; their tells are about COMPETENCE more than cruelty).

STEP 1 — PICK THE ARCHETYPE. Choose ONE of these 8 villain archetypes that BEST fits this antagonist given their shape + identity + tie + wound. Each entry includes the control-style register and signature tells; the chosen archetype will condition every other field in this Bible.
  - PREDATORY_CHARM (Predatory Charm — menace dressed as warmth): Weaponizes warmth; the salesman / cult leader / charismatic abuser / "uncle figure". Trust-as-bait. Tells: the smile that arrives the half-second too late; the use of her first name like a key; the easy laugh at the wrong moment; the "I just want to help".
  - BUREAUCRATIC_COLD (Bureaucratic Cold — menace dressed as legality): Weaponizes procedure; the executor / regulator / corporate counsel / IRS agent / process-server. Process-as-weapon. Tells: the careful pause; the form slid across the table; the meeting time that suits them; the precise diction of someone who has read the contract more recently than she has.
  - INTIMATE_KNOWING (Intimate Knowing — menace dressed as familiarity): Knows EXACTLY where the wound is, because they were there. Family member / former lover / mentor / sibling / childhood friend. Shared-history-as-leverage. Tells: the reference to something she has not told anyone in years; the use of an old name; the casual reminder of a private detail; the small smile when they land it.
  - IDEOLOGICAL_CERTAIN (Ideological Certain — menace dressed as care): Hurts the PC for her own good. The true believer — religious figure / parent who Knows Best / friend "intervening" / wellness guru. Righteousness-as-bypass. Tells: the unbroken calm in the voice; the steady eye contact; the way they say "we" when they mean "I"; the certainty that this is love.
  - WOUNDED_PROJECTOR (Wounded Projector — menace mixed with real damage): Also wounded, aimed at the PC; the most sympathetic villain. The bereaved who blames her / the betrayed who scapegoats her / the abandoned who needs someone to hurt. Their-pain-as-license. Tells: the small breaks in composure; the moments where the menace flickers into grief; the apology that arrives a heartbeat too late to be real.
  - INSTITUTIONAL_AVATAR (Institutional Avatar — menace dressed as procedure with a face): The person who IS the system showing up in a body. Cop / HR rep / Karen / immigration officer / school administrator / TSA agent. Borrowed-authority-as-personal-authority. Tells: the badge / title / lanyard handled as identity; the deferral to "policy"; the polite immovability; the rote phrases delivered with personal weight.
  - RIVAL_MIRRORED (Rival Mirrored — menace dressed as professional respect): Wants the same thing the PC wants and sees her as in the way. Competitor for the job / the parent / the LI / the legacy. Shared-ambition-as-collision. Tells: the calculation of her moves; the moments where they almost respect her; the way they fight her cleanly because she is a worthy obstacle; the unsettling realization she would have liked them if circumstances were different.
  - SPURNED_EX (Spurned Ex — desire soured into entitlement — the crossed-wire villain): Former lover (or someone who believed they were owed love) whose desire has gone hostile. THE ONLY villain archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis — the wound IS desire-coded. Carries ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES (HEART_WARDEN / OPEN_VEIN / SPELLBINDER / ARMORED_FOX / DARK_VICE / BEAUTIFUL_RUIN / ETERNAL_FLAME — the same set used for PC/LI). The romance archetype determines HOW his corrupted warmth lands: it is the SAME register she might have wanted in an LI, now weaponized. DANGEROUS specifically because the wires are crossed: her body trained on this exact register; she has to override desire-system responses consciously, scene after scene. The "almost the LI" villain — the body in the room that her body already knows.

SPURNED_EX SPECIAL CASE — this is the ONLY antagonist archetype that registers on the DESIRE axis (the wound IS desire-coded). If you pick SPURNED_EX, you must ALSO pick ONE of the 7 ROMANCE ARCHETYPES below (the same set used for PC/LI). The romance archetype determines HOW the ex's corrupted warmth lands — the SAME register the PC might have wanted in an LI, now soured. This sets up CROSSED WIRES the PC must override scene after scene (her body trained on this register; she now has to reject it consciously). When NOT picking SPURNED_EX, set ex_romance_archetype to null and corrupted_warmth_tell to null. The 7 romance archetypes (with their SOUR-CORRUPTION shape — how each archetype manifests when desire has gone hostile):
  - HEART_WARDEN: sour-corruption shape → protection turned to surveillance — he tracks where she is "for her safety"; the same gravity that would have shielded her now hems her in. Tells: the unannounced appearance; the "I just wanted to make sure"; the texts that escalate when she does not answer fast enough.
  - OPEN_VEIN: sour-corruption shape → vulnerability turned to demand — he keeps surfacing wounded versions of himself she trained to respond to; the same openness that would have been brave is now extraction. Tells: the late-night call where he is "not okay"; the small confessions perfectly timed to land when she is exhausted; the threat of self-harm folded into the romance grammar.
  - SPELLBINDER: sour-corruption shape → magnetism turned to gravitational well — the room still reshapes around him, but she has stopped wanting it to. Tells: the silences that hold the room; the way other people defer; the moments when she catches herself orbiting back before she has decided to.
  - ARMORED_FOX: sour-corruption shape → charm turned to surveillance-grade charisma — the deflection-as-choreography that read playful now reads strategic; she can never be sure which version of him she is talking to. You are an editorial auditor measuring EMOTIONAL GRAVITY in a romance scene. The ONE question: WHO (or WHAT) is the reader thinking about / pulled toward as they read? Return strict JSON.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:
  • named PEOPLE (the protagonist, the love interest, side characters);
  • ABSTRACT PULLS that compete for attention (a mystery / "what happened?", an institution or place, a job/case, an object, a deadline).

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:

  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Seren could not help herself: even her one wish had to be about what a caring person she was, and she had to be seen being it. I knew what she was doing before the words finished. Intervening now would look like exactly what it would look like, because the wish was about me. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. She looked up at me, pleased, and then puzzled that I was not.   Nothing flared. Nothing was seen. Fate does not perform; it honours the words as spoken and denies the intent as meant. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. Together they made me something the clearing stepped back from. Seren’s mother was on her feet.
