At least she spared me some embarrassment by blurring the wound instead of naming it. “So that Lirael may find the one she lost.” It was the beautiful mistake.   I heard it the instant the words left her: not a wrong note but a loose one, a wish described too gently to bind. Every First Favored in the clearing heard it a breath after I did. A Weave-Script stuttered on a guest’s throat. One hand stopped mid-gesture. The Dohkar went still. I was sealed. I was forbidden to interfere. Intervening now would look like exactly what it would look like, because the wish was about me. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. She looked up at me, pleased, and then puzzled that I was not.   Nothing flared. Nothing was seen. Fate does not perform; it honours the words as spoken and denies the intent as meant. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. Either would have ended it: Dohkar this morning, Chayr, Provast one day, the path my father had walked and I had never once imagined not walking. Together they made me something the clearing stepped back from. Seren’s mother was on her feet. And still, with my standing coming down around me, some traitorous part of my attention went to the edge of the gathering, to the man who had not moved. I did not want him to look away. I wanted, God help me, to be the thing he was looking at.   Julian moved. He came in from the edge without hurry, and the assembly made room for him the way rooms do for a man who has never asked them to. The Dohkar’s Weave-Script went a hard, flat colour that said, whether he liked it or not, that he had noticed who they deferred to. “I can hear where she is aligned,” Julian said, to all of them and to me. “Everything in her points one way. She believes she did not do this.” He did not say what had been done, or by whom. He drew out The Answer — the double-ended shaft, a deep hooked blade curling from each end like a question asked twice — and set it in my hands, and closed my fingers around it with his, the scarred wrist against my palm for one deliberate second. “Hold it. I am going to ask you questions, here, in front of them. If you are misaligned when you answer, everyone present will know.” It lay still between my hands. My mouth was uncovered now. I found I still could not speak.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind.   • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.

  - IDEOLOGICAL_CERTAIN (Ideological Certain — menace dressed as care): Hurts the PC for her own good. Tells: the unbroken calm in the voice; the steady eye contact; the way they say "we" when they mean "I"; the certainty that this is love.

Tells: the calculation of her moves; the moments where they almost respect her; the way they fight her cleanly because she is a worthy obstacle; the unsettling realization she would have liked them if circumstances were different.

  - SPELLBINDER: sour-corruption shape → magnetism turned to gravitational well — the room still reshapes around him, but she has stopped wanting it to. Tells: the silences that hold the room; the way other people defer; the moments when she catches herself orbiting back before she has decided to.

The Provast — the office my father had held before him, over every Chayr in the Veilwood , and the man next in line for First Dohkar. Present as an observer only, and observing me. He never crossed a floor first. He had let clearings full of people come to him for twenty years and called it patience, and I — who cannot stand at the edge of anything without my whole face announcing it — could not tell whether what he was withholding from me was a feeling or the fact that there wasn’t one. My father used to say Julian saw everything in a room and offered none of it, and let people call that discretion because it cost him nothing. I had noticed him the way you notice a change in the light, before I knew what I was noticing. I made myself look back at my ward. Along my own arms the Weave-Script stayed the colour I wanted it to be, and I was proud of that for exactly as long as it lasted.   Seren began the invocation. I knew every word of it, and for the space of three of them I was not afraid. Then she looked up at me — not at the Dohkar, not at her mother — and I watched her decide. She abandoned the practiced wish. She knew the rule; she had recited it back to me for months. In front of the whole assembly she spent her First Sacrifice on me instead. Seren could not help herself: even her one wish had to be about what a caring person she was, and she had to be seen being it. I knew what she was doing before the words finished. I have never in my life been able to keep a feeling off my face, and it has taught me exactly what one looks like when it has been arranged there. At least she spared me some embarrassment by blurring the wound instead of naming it. “So that Lirael may find the one she lost.” It was the beautiful mistake.   I heard it the instant the words left her: not a wrong note but a loose one, a wish described too gently to bind. Every First Favored in the clearing heard it a breath after I did. A Weave-Script stuttered on a guest’s throat. One hand stopped mid-gesture. The Dohkar went still. I was sealed. I was forbidden to interfere. Intervening now would look like exactly what it would look like, because the wish was about me. I tore the band away and moved toward her anyway. “Seren —” The first word I had spoken aloud since the sash went on, and it was already too late to be anything but evidence. She looked up at me, pleased, and then puzzled that I was not.   Nothing flared. Nothing was seen. Fate does not perform; it honours the words as spoken and denies the intent as meant. Seren had asked that I find the one I lost, and what was found, in that clearing, was the loss itself — two dozen faces turning to me at once, looking for it, reading the torn band and the step I had taken and the sash that said whose rite this was. “‘Find.’” The presiding Dohkar named the word, because he cannot let a lesson pass. “She asked that you find the one you lost. Fate did not go looking. It made every one of us look at you.” Then the charges, laid in the order he thought them: that the wish had been shaped for its supervisor’s benefit — coerced, or worse, taught — and that the supervisor had broken her seal and interfered in her own ward’s rite. Either would have ended it: Dohkar this morning, Chayr, Provast one day, the path my father had walked and I had never once imagined not walking. Together they made me something the clearing stepped back from. Seren’s mother was on her feet. And still, with my standing coming down around me, some traitorous part of my attention went to the edge of the gathering, to the man who had not moved. I did not want him to look away. I wanted, God help me, to be the thing he was looking at.   Julian moved. He came in from the edge without hurry, and the assembly made room for him the way rooms do for a man who has never asked them to. The Dohkar’s Weave-Script went a hard, flat colour that said, whether he liked it or not, that he had noticed who they deferred to. “I can hear where she is aligned,” Julian said, to all of them and to me. “Everything in her points one way. She believes she did not do this.” He did not say what had been done, or by whom. He drew out The Answer — the double-ended shaft, a deep hooked blade curling from each end like a question asked twice — and set it in my hands, and closed my fingers around it with his, the scarred wrist against my palm for one deliberate second. “Hold it. I am going to ask you questions, here, in front of them. If you are misaligned when you answer, everyone present will know.” It lay still between my hands. My mouth was uncovered now. I found I still could not speak.

You are the SCENE-SPINE planner for an interactive romance engine. The scene has ONE organizing event: a STATE CHANGE — an irreversible, externally observable event that flips a specific fact from FALSE to TRUE. Everything else in the scene serves it. First name the TACTICAL MOVE (what this scene does to advance the current milestone — an input constraint, NOT the event), then express it as a state_change per the CONTRACT.
STATE_CHANGE CONTRACT (HARD — reused from the proven Scene-1 primitive, do NOT soften):
  • state_change_precondition: ONE sentence naming the single fact NOT YET TRUE when the scene opens — the "before", the negation of the state_change, phrased so the scene must OPEN with it still false. 8-16 words.
  • state_change: the observable EVENT, landing partway through, that flips the precondition FALSE→TRUE, witnessed on-page. HARD REQUIREMENTS: (a) it makes the precondition true — do NOT restate anything already true at the opening; (b) EXTERNALLY OBSERVABLE — an event another character in the room could WITNESS happen, NOT a private feeling or realization ("she realizes the chain is alive" is INVALID; "the chain recoils from his hand, links contracting" is VALID); (c) it CHANGES SOMETHING IN THE WORLD — you must be able to say WHO loses WHAT immediately, or what is now true that was not; an emotional realization or a shift in mood is NOT a state_change — answer "what changed in the world?", never "how does she feel?"; (d) NAME ONLY THE EVENT — STOP AT THE CONCRETE MOMENT; everything after "revealing…", "making her realize…", "as she understands…" is BANNED (that appended interpretation makes the renderer write a flat "X becomes visible, revealing a deeper truth" summary instead of staging the moment). 8-16 words, phrased as the event.
  • forces_choice: the decision the event UNLOCKS — the scene's closing choice, which could NOT have been posed before it (the event exists to CREATE this choice). "forces [PC] to choose between A and B" where A and B are TWO ACTIVE responses to the new fact (NOT one action + one escape hatch like "act or do nothing").
  • SPECIFICITY (HARD — the state_change must UNIQUELY identify THIS milestone): realize the milestone's SPECIFIC concrete content — its named objects, places, and actions — NOT a generic version of the theme. If the milestone names "a submerged bell that rings for their bond", the event must involve THAT bell ("the submerged bell tolls once beneath the water"); do NOT abstract it to "their bond glows" / "the thread pulses" / "the vow binds them". SPECIFICITY TEST: hide the milestone text and show ONLY your state_change — a reader must be able to point to WHICH milestone it came from. If your event could equally belong to a DIFFERENT milestone in this arc, or to "their bond" in general, it has FAILED — rewrite it using the milestone's OWN nouns and actions.
  • forces_choice — NO ESCAPE HATCH (HARD): both branches must be ACTIVE responses to the new fact. "reject it / retreat / flee / wait / do nothing / walk away / leave" are opt-outs — if EITHER branch is an opt-out, the choice is INVALID; both must be things the PC DOES about the new reality. Provide branch_a and branch_b explicitly.
  • DELETE TEST (the sufficiency invariant — the state_change is valid ONLY if it passes): delete the event, and BOTH branch_a AND branch_b become impossible or materially different. If either branch would still stand unchanged without the event, the event is too weak — pick a stronger one.

Allocate EXACTLY 100 points of READER ATTENTION across the entities and abstract pulls in the scene. An entity's share = how much of the reader's emotional bandwidth it occupies (presence on the page × emotional charge), NOT mere word count. Include:

CRITICAL — PRESENCE IS NOT GRAVITY (Roman 2026-06-02). An OFFSTAGE love interest can still hold high gravity if the prose makes the reader LONG FOR / DREAD / OBSESS OVER / RESENT / ANTICIPATE / be FASCINATED BY him. "Why am I thinking about him?" is gravity even when he is not in the room. Do NOT dock the love interest for being offstage; score the actual pull the prose generates toward him. Likewise a PRESENT love interest who is just furniture (described but not charged) scores LOW.

For the love interest specifically, also classify the KIND of gravity (if any): longing / fascination / dread / resentment / curiosity / anticipation / obsession / jealousy / denial / NONE.

VERDICT on the love interest as a gravity source:
  LEAD     — the love interest is THE dominant pull, or co-dominant; the reader is primarily thinking about him.
  PRESENT  — the love interest is a real but secondary pull; something else (mystery/place/side-character) dominates.
  ABSENT   — the love interest is not a meaningful source of gravity; the scene's pull is elsewhere entirely. THIS IS THE ROMANCE-LEAD FAILURE regardless of his presence mode.

ALSO re-bucket the same 100 points into engine CATEGORIES (this is what we actually control): love_interest, protagonist, relationship (the bond/tension BETWEEN them), relationship_mystery (intrigue INSIDE the relationship — why did HE do this / what happened between THEM — this is R-PLOT, not A-plot), plot_mystery (intrigue about the EXTERNAL situation — A-PLOT), a_plot_logistics, side_characters, other. These also sum to ~100. R-PLOT engine = love_interest + protagonist + relationship + relationship_mystery; A-PLOT engine = plot_mystery + a_plot_logistics. A relationship-first scene puts ~80% on the R-plot engine even if procedural words appear — judge GRAVITY, not vocabulary. NOTE: the relationship can generate its OWN mystery/suspense/danger; do not reflexively file intrigue as A-plot.

FINALLY — the DESIRE REGISTER (Roman 2026-06-02, the deepest metric). Relationship gravity is NOT the same as DESIRE. A scene can put 80% on the relationship and still be emotionally COLD — running on grief, regret, wound-rumination, and reflection rather than WANTING. The protagonist can be thinking ABOUT the love interest (analysis, mourning, meaning-making) without WANTING him (attraction, longing-now, curiosity, hunger, obsession, need). These produce radically different romance novels. Measure the PC's emotional energy-toward-the-LI: how much is HOT (wanting) vs COLD (elegiac)? An honest read — if the scene is sad/wounded/reflective, say COLD even if the relationship is omnipresent. "Nobody wants anybody" is the failure this metric exists to catch.

AND THE DEEPEST CUT — the DESIRE TARGET. Even when desire is present, WHERE does it point? The core pathology is the love interest functioning as a mystery-CONTAINER (sender of the money, keeper of the secret, target of the investigation) rather than a PERSON. The reader of a great romance asks "what is WRONG with him / what is he hiding from ME / why can't I stop thinking about him" — they want HIM. The failure asks "what is in the folder / who sent the money" — they want the ANSWER, and the LI is just the box it is locked in. Judge honestly what the protagonist is actually WANTING: him (the person), or plot-truth / her own closure / her own self-understanding. If her attention to him is entirely "what does his action MEAN for the plot," that is PLOT_TRUTH, not ROMAN — say so.

FINALLY — ROMAN:MODE. Whatever share of attention the love interest holds, decompose its KIND. He can hold gravity while OFFSTAGE — that is fine (Darcy, Christian, Han all do) — but the gravity must be the RIGHT kind. Allocate 100 points of HIS gravity (his share, normalized to 100) across these eight modes:
  • PLOT_OBJECT — he is a piece on the board: the sender of the money, the subject of the case, the man whose scheme matters. Interest in his PLOT FUNCTION.
  • REPUTATION — she relates to what she has HEARD of him / his public image / the story about him, not to him.
  • CURIOSITY — she wants to KNOW him: who is he really, why did he do this, what is under the armor. (Curiosity about the PERSON, not the plot-answer.)
  • ATTRACTION — she is drawn to him bodily / wants him / notices him as a man.
  • DESIRE — active wanting / longing for him now.
  • OBSESSION — she cannot stop thinking about HIM specifically.
  • RESENTMENT — charged grievance toward him (can be erotic).
  • FEAR — he frightens her (can be charged).
The WANTING-HIM cluster (the goal) = CURIOSITY + ATTRACTION + DESIRE + OBSESSION. The OBJECT cluster (the failure) = PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION. Be honest: "why did he send the money / what is his scheme" is PLOT_OBJECT; "why do I still know his handwriting / why can't I stop thinking about him" is OBSESSION/CURIOSITY. A scene can score the LI high and have it be ENTIRELY PLOT_OBJECT + REPUTATION — that is the disease in its purest form.
